newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel government intact after prosecutor report.
newsitem.headline: Israel government intact after prosecutor report.

text.p: Israel's government survived intact after prosecutors decided not to charge Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for lack of evidence despite their "real suspicions" about his role in a corruption scandal.
The affair had sidelined efforts to pull the Middle East peace process out of a deep crisis sparked when Israel began work on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March.

State Attorney Edna Arbel told a news conference some of her prosecution colleagues had wanted to indict Netanyahu and Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi over the short-lived appointment of an attorney general in January.

But prosecutors finally decided that only Netanyahu's political ally Aryeh Deri, already facing corruption charges, should be indicted and his director-general, Avigdor Lieberman, should face further investigation.

Communications Minister Limor Livnat and Finance Minister Dan Meridor of Netanyahu's Likud party and two small parties key to the government coalition, all of whom had considered resigning, said they would remain in the government after Arbel's report.
The main opposition Labour party called for Netanyahu's resignation, but Livnat told Israel Channel One television the important point was that Netanyahu "didn't have any criminal intentions."

Labour legislator Yossi Beilin, using Netanyahu's nickname, said: "A criminal tonight would be satisfied, a prime minister would resign and Bibi has to decide if he is a criminal or a prime minister."
Netanyahu, 47, said in a televised speech immediately after prosecutors issued their 75-page report: "The bottom line is I didn't commit any crime and the attorney general confirmed that."
He apologised for any mistakes in the January appointment, but he lashed out at the media and opposition which he said had used the affair "to overthrow the government."

Hundreds of supporters of Deri's religious Shas party attacked a Channel One crew outside Shas party mentor Rabbi Ovadia Yosef's Jerusalem home late on Sunday, hurling stones and shouting "Death to the media," the station said.

A Channel One report spurred the original police inquiry into the appointment of Likud party activist and lawyer Roni Bar-On as attorney general. It alleged Deri coerced the government into appointing Bar-On, who would then offer him a plea bargain.
Bar-On quit 12 hours after taking office amid a public outcry that he was a legal lightweight unqualified for the job.
Police recommended that Netanyahu, in office for 11 months, should be indicted for fraud and breach of trust.

Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani's Third Way party, which has four seats in the 120-member parliament, had debated withdrawing from the coalition but he said after the report: "I am happy the matter is behind us."

The Israel B'Aliya party, with seven seats, had also threatened to leave. Israel television quoted it as deciding: "The report does not justify bringing down the government but there is a need, and I quote, 'for a drastic change in the way decisions are taken by the government'."
Israel Radio said Meridor had also decided to remain, allowing Netanyahu to continue to command 66 parliamentary seats.
Education Minister Zvulun Hammer, of the National Religious Party, said: "I think the government has the right to exist. It isn't any worse than others from the moral point of view."
But two legislators from Labour and the left-wing Meretz party said they would appeal to the High Court to order charges to be brought against Netanyahu and Hanegbi.
